reviews.text: Are We There Yet? In the interest of full disclosure up front, I'll do my best to assess this release without being overly unkind. To be honest, this debut feature from writer-director Alexander Ullom has almost assuredly earned itself a spot on my "Worst of 2026" list. Loosely based on the 1944 existentialist stage play No Exit by Jean-Paul Sartre, "It Ends" tells the story of four twenty-something friends (a term I use loosely) (Phinehas Yoon, Mitchell Cole, Akira Jackson, Noah Toth) who embark on a late-night drive but soon find themselves lost on a never-ending highway through a thickly forested woodland from which there's no apparent escape (i.e., "no exit"). In an effort to spice up the plot, the narrative subsequently attempts to infuse a few horror tropes, but, sadly, these poorly handled elements aren't particularly scary or the least bit enlightening in defining the essence of the plot. (At one point, for instance, the puzzled quartet is attacked by a band of fleet-footed zombies, forcing the fearful foursome to flee for their lives. It's an element that's reincorporated or inferred throughout the film but that, frankly, has little ultimate bearing on the story. What's more, the sequence is so ineptly executed that it's ultimately more confusing than frightening.) Not long thereafter, when matters settle down and these lost souls begin discussing the nature of their bewildering circumstances, they're forced to begin considering that they might be trapped in some kind of alternate existence, even a hellish version of the afterlife. That possibility, in turn, prompts yet another round of long-winded, uninteresting existential discussions that are part metaphysics, part petty bickering and part overwrought Generation Z angst, all set against the backdrop of an incessant road trip for which practical concerns like having enough fuel for the journey (wherever it may be headed) are apparently irrelevant. And that, in a nutshell, fittingly characterizes the dynamics of this wholly pretentious offering, despite what may have started out with a worthwhile premise and good intentions. The blame here lies largely with the woefully undercooked, meandering screenplay. For example, most of the excessive group discussions are lame and unfocused and lack engaging substance, light years removed from the eloquence and insight of the source material that inspired this production. Then there's the seriously underused horror aspect, which might have added more interest if more skillfully and integrally employed. The filming techniques are also stunningly puzzling, with much of the action shot too dimly and/or too up-close, so much so that, in sequences like the zombie attack, it's difficult to tell what's happening. And, of course, there are plot holes aplenty, which are genuinely inexcusable, even for a first-time filmmaker. To its credit, though, the picture gets one thing right: it's a testament to Sartre's renowned contention that "hell is other people," as these characters come to find out for themselves, bringing fresh meaning to that statement and to the audience (indeed, I can't imagine being stuck with individuals like these for eternity; 89 minutes was more than enough for me). But that spot-on irony is not nearly enough to save this effort, especially since it even more ironically gives viewers reason to skip this release. Perhaps, as a senior, the generational nuances at work here were lost on me, but, that aside, while screening this offering, I also couldn't help but keep asking myself, "Are we there yet?"

But hey it's about the journey with these asexual Turdburgling Gen Zers not the destination. But have you ever had an actual Cliff Bar?? Puke. I'm glad they made this movie and it exists bc I now get to weed out people with a social filter who loved it and want to explain why we didn't get it are. So thanks for that. Great name though, bc that's all your asking the whole damn movie after the first 15. Tyler made a great call to go act in an other movie early.

reviews.author: JoyeuxJardinier
reviews.text: "I never should have smoked that sh*t. Now I'm on the endless road." This is not your typical "friends drive into the woods" horror setup. No cabin, no sex, no wrong detour. Just four friends trapped in a car, and a brutally simple premise - almost similar to The Long Walk: keep moving or something worse than death happens. No soldiers here - just a creeping menace. Every pause invites something unnamed to stir in the forest. Figures appear. Murmurs rise. Screams smear into the soundscape. The design is insanely effective. The title card itself feels like a threat - strobing, aggressive, vaguely Gaspar Noé-coded. Visually, it reminded me of It Follows, especially in those circling shots where you scan the tree line for movement, waiting for silhouettes to emerge from the dark. Going in, I actually thought It Ends was some kind of sequel. IT FOLLOWS / IT ENDS - same typography, come on. Exit 8 also hovers in the background, with its looping logic, disorienting repetition and existential puzzle. Add deadpan humor and road-trip nihilism, and somehow the film becomes funny and terrifying at the same time - and weirdly profound. The camera mostly stays inside the car: tight close-ups, faces pressed against windows, dashboard lights flickering. When it does escape the car, it's only to remind us that the woods are both vast and suffocating - and the trees merely bars around their glass-and-metal cage. I finished this movie as the sun was coming up, which felt right. For whatever it was, I enjoyed this road trip. And yeah - I'd ride with this crew again. SPOILERS START HERE. No hunger, no thirst, no fuel anxiety. These absences quietly nudge the film toward a "purgatory fable" reading. Funny enough, I recently watched Eden, which - despite being a true story - I also viewed as a fable: archetypal humans, like minor gods stuck on Mount Olympus, trapped on a "purgatory island" where hell is other people. Here, it's different. This is The Myth of Sisyphus on wheels. Camus' concept of the absurd, pushed to metaphysical extremes - not an abstract idea, but a lived condition. Endless motion. No explanation. No payoff. What really keeps the film alive isn't the mystery - it's the characters grinding against it. As in Eden, where each household represented a way of being human - the philosopher, the builder, the performer -, each character here embodies a different response to the absurd: Tyler is despair incarnate: "Can't keep worrying about sh*t that don't end". He looks into the void and says Nope. No Sisyphus here - why push the rock? James is pure reason - "The answer is forward". He believes - against all evidence - that logic and motion will crack the mystery. When the car won't start, he spirals over the road not taken. The not-knowing is what keeps him moving. Day and Fish adapt. They're the lifeforce. They ritualize, set rules ("No anger in the f*cking car"), invent games, scream, dance, and learn Spanish from car manuals. They're not solving the problem - they're surviving it. Fish nails it early on: "No offense, T. Real life seems like it sucks *ss." The movie clearly doesn't want to take sides or explain itself - it wants to watch you cope. The ending worked for me - frustrating, yet absolutely on point. Maybe the destination was never the issue. Maybe it was always the ride - and who you are stuck riding with.
reviews.summary: "I never should have smoked that sh*t. Now I'm on the endless road."

reviews.author: Jeroenymus_
reviews.text: New David Lynch? I'm giving the film a 10. Not because it's technically perfect, but mainly because it features an original and highly mythical script. Actually, something new, refreshing, and interesting is emerging from a country normally dominated by superficial Hollywood productions. Has the new David Lynch perhaps emerged? I'd much rather see a film like this, which might not be technically perfect, but offers a story that far surpasses the average blockbuster, which has the depth of a surfboard. The cast, while perhaps not as experienced, clearly has potential and empathizes more than their overpaid Hollywood counterparts. And if anyone in particular stands out, it's Mitchell Cole. He has a fantastic monotone voice and great stage presence. Watching this film, I felt the same way I did when I saw Sam Raimi's first film (Within the Woods/Evil Dead 1) from 1979/1980. Super original and innovative camera techniques. The same thing happens here, but in terms of the script. However, I hope the director/writer of "It Ends" doesn't follow the same (commercial) path as Sam Raimi.

reviews.author: gerbildad
reviews.text: The most existential movie I've ever seen It's not surprising that so many people give this movie a low rating. People who are looking for thrills and scares and gore and nudity will find little to enjoy here. No, this is a thinking person's movie. (Spoilers) It starts out with the usual banter and swearing from a suitably diverse cast. So far, so good! Then it takes a very strange turn (or rather, it DOESN'T turn). The road does not end and doesn't seem to go anywhere. Every time they stop, they're attacked by zombie-like people who come running out of the woods. The car runs on and on, strangely without needing fuel or maintenance. The people have no biological urges. The four of them have a range of responses from acceptance to analysis to panic. After driving for some 50,000 miles, Tyler decides he doesn't want to do that anymore and leaves the group (existential choice #1!). He goes off into the woods. What will happen to him? We never find out, nor does it really matter; he has made his choice. After more than a million miles, Day and Fisher decide they can't take it anymore and snatch the car keys from the ignition. They are giving up (existential choice #2!). They try to convince James to give up as well, but he defies them and manages to start the car again (existential choice #3!) He drives on, believing that he will eventually get somewhere. Finally, the road ends. There are a large number of cars parked in and around a cul-de-sac. (Most of these are late model cars. Does this mean anything, or is it a budgetary restriction? I don't know.) So, James' dream comes to nothing. He finally screams--something he had repeatedly refused to do. Then he nibbles on the candy bar that they didn't eat earlier, and finds it unbelievably tasty. He decides to get back in the car and head back the other way (existential choice #4!). On the way, he finds the comatose driver of another abandoned car and puts him in the passenger's seat. James asks the hypothetical question that dogged the group since the beginning: who would win: 50 hawks or a man with a gun? The man stirs from his torpor and responds that the hawks would tear the man apart. In this way, meaning is found in trivial things (another existential theme). Thus, this movie explores different ways to react when you realize life is ultimately meaningless. Ultimately, you have to make your own meaning (Existentialism incarnate!). So, what happened? Why are they in this situation? We never find out, but that's not the point. The point is the different way the characters react. Interestingly, the wildly varying number of stars itself explores the existential question: how would you react to a movie that seems meaningless?
reviews.summary: The most existential movie I've ever seen

reviews.text: Existential dread and snappy dialogue? Sign me up! Intro: It Ends is director (and writer! Wow, you go, guy!) Alex Ullom's first feature-length film, and what a fantastic first entry. Do you like existential, cerebral horror? Do you often find yourself going through the motions of life and constantly questioning if the journey you're on is worth it? Do you wake up at 6 in the morning and take that cold stare at yourself in the mirror, frosting the glass with your abated breath, just thinking to yourself, "Why am I even doing this for?" Well, if you said yes to any of these questions, then this movie is a treat for you! Summary: Three fresh college grads are picked up by their long-time high-school friend to head back home on what would seem to be just a generic, coming-of-age story about reflecting on one's future after college. Until one wrong turn takes them on a never-ending journey into a bizarre almost never-ending road as they're chased by hordes of desperate people trying to escape that very same prison. The story follows the plight of certified tough and designated leader Tyler played by Mitchell Cole, aimless Pals Day (Akira Jackson) and Fisher (Noah Toth), and their blunt and posturing future systems engineer James as they traverse this seemingly never-ending road, trying to gather their bearings and find a way out of this dreary yet verdant Purgatory. We watch our heroes not necessarily survive but learn to adapt to their new world, each in their own specific ways. Tyler's approach is to tough out the trip, never unveiling his true anxieties and fears, eventually culminating in him being the first departure for the group, setting the tone for the rest of the film as the rest of the troupe now must try to figure out how to fend for themselves without their faithful leader, leaving James to be the most affected by this loss. Day and Fisher's approach is to accept the pointless endeavor of their journey and establish concrete routines and boundaries to ensure their mental and physical well-being. While our reluctant hero James decides to view the entire scenario as an elaborate puzzle or test, given to them in order to learn an invisible answer that never quite reveals itself. And yes, if any of these wonderfully deep and fleshed-out characters, with their natural banter and camaraderie feel familiar, it's because it is. Not in the "woah, they like me for real" type of way but in a deeply personal "wow, this is how I approach life" kind of way. The film goes to great lengths just to show how each of these approaches are both valid and flawed at the same time. Tyler's brute force method was good to start the adventure, and his silent show of strength gave a sense of stability to the rest of the group. However, we see that this avoidance of talking about his problems bubbled over inside of him until he could no longer take the incessant traveling and chose to end his journey on his own terms. Day and Fisher's approach gives a much-needed and healthy routine to give themselves a sense of stability through creating reliable means of expressing themselves, getting exercise, and setting boundaries for themselves yet, they're also just going through the motions. Could complacency really be an answer to the existential never-ending road we also walk on? And lastly, James' approach of constant vigilance, problem solving, and plan setting did ultimately get him the furthest toward the "goal" of escape. The story follows the plight of Tyler, a "blue-collar type...and unspoken leader of the group" ('It Ends' Review - Inventive Horror Hangout Movie Gets Existential, written by Meagan Navarro of Bloody Disgusting), played by Mitchell Cole; aimless Pals Day (Akira Jackson) and Fisher (Noah Toth); and their blunt and posturing future systems engineer James (Phinehas Yoon), as they traverse this seemingly endless road, trying to gather their bearings and find a way out of this dreary yet verdant Purgatory. We watch our heroes not necessarily survive, but learn to adapt to their new world, each in their own specific way. Tyler's approach is to tough out the trip, never revealing his true anxieties and fears, eventually culminating in him being the first to depart from the group, setting the tone for the rest of the film as the troupe must figure out how to fend for themselves without their faithful leader. Day and Fisher's approach is to accept the pointlessness of their endeavor and establish concrete routines and boundaries to ensure their mental and physical well-being. Meanwhile, our reluctant hero James views the entire scenario as an elaborate puzzle or test, designed to teach an invisible answer that never quite reveals itself. If any of these wonderfully deep and fleshed-out characters, with their natural banter and camaraderie, feel familiar, it's because they do. Not in the "woah, they like me for real" type of way, but in a deeply personal "wow, this is how I approach life" kind of way. The film goes to great lengths to show how each traveler's approach is both valid and flawed at the same time. Tyler's brute-force method was effective at the start of the adventure, and his silent show of strength gave a sense of stability to the rest of the group. However, this avoidance of talking about his problems eventually bubbled over until he could no longer endure the incessant traveling, choosing to end his journey on his own terms by exiting the vehicle, leaving James the most affected by this loss. Day and Fisher's approach provides a much-needed and healthy routine to create a sense of stability through reliable means of expression, exercise, and boundary-setting for their trip. However, I have problems with this approach as well as they are doing what's considered healthy and normal in modern society but they're also just going through the motions. Can complacency really be the best approach to the existential never-ending road we call life? Is living life without any real purpose actually meaningful? Great coping mechanism yes, but a solution? I'm not really sure. Lastly, James' approach of constant vigilance, problem solving, and plan setting ultimately gets him the furthest toward the "goal" of escape they all sought. However, this also leads him to abandon Day and Fisher to continue the journey, only to reach a literal Dead End (see what I did there 😉?). This reveal definitely seemed to be divisive amongst viewers because, upon reaching the end of the road, James ends up driving back the opposite way to find the friends he left behind, picking up a new companion and starting the same conversation he had with his friends at the beginning of the film. So, what was the point of the movie, if it had a point at all? Analysis: Truthfully, I don't believe any of these approaches (and, for that matter, my personal take lol) are right nor are they wrong. They're just simply different, common approaches to life that we see everyone take. I absolutely loved that even at the end of the road we see that SO MANY CARS have also reached this point as well, with no passengers inside them, leaving us, the viewer, to believe they all succumbed to the odd fate expected from everyone on this road, becoming zombies who only awaken upon hearing of other people who may provide them a means of escape, only to be relegated back to dormancy once this means of escape disappears. Because, yeah, life is bleak, it is seemingly endless, and it often times never gives you the straight answer you're looking for. Likes and dislikes: I'll just get this out of the way, I had no dislikes for this film. I rarely (yeah, I know this is my second review, let me cook, dang it!) rate films 5 stars. The only other film that I'd rate 5 stars is Life is Beautiful, and it's BECAUSE IT'S LIFE IS BEAUTIFUL (go watch it! Written and also directed by the lead actor Roberto Benigni). So, here goes my glazing session for this film: Cinematography: Same as above, no dislikes and all five stars. Acting: Listen, have you heard of any of these names before? Let me play it back for ya: Mitchell Cole (Tyler), Akira Jackson (Pals Day), Noah Toth (Fisher), and Phinehas Yoon (James) REMEMBER THESE NAMES because I have never seen such a talented young cast. They all nailed their roles. I loved the aloof, blunt directness Phinehas gave his James. I loved the stoic, quiet strength, with subtle vulnerability Mitchell gave Tyler, and I absolutely ADORED the heart and warmth Akira and Noah gave their Day and Fisher. If the phrase is "to chew a scene," then these peeps FEASTED. Dialogue: Listen, have you heard of any of these names before? Let me play it back for ya: Mitchell Cole (Tyler), Akira Jackson (Pals Day), Noah Toth (Fisher), and Phinehas Yoon (James) REMEMBER THESE NAMES because I have never seen such a talented young cast. They all nailed their roles. They delivered each line with precision, emotion, and presence. Bonus: I'd be remiss if I didn't mention how much I LOVE that this film does not shy away from its obvious inspiration: Dead End. I'm not going to say more than that since this review is already pretty lengthy, but you should also definitely give that film a watch too!

And yes, if any of these wonderfully deep and fleshed-out characters, with their natural banter and camaraderie feel familiar, it's because it is. Not in the "woah, they like me for real" type of way but in a deeply personal "wow, this is how I approach life" kind of way. The film goes to great lengths just to show how each of these approaches are both valid and flawed at the same time. Tyler's brute force method was good to start the adventure, and his silent show of strength gave a sense of stability to the rest of the group. However, we see that this avoidance of talking about his problems bubbled over inside of him until he could no longer take the incessant traveling and chose to end his journey on his own terms. Day and Fisher's approach gives a much-needed and healthy routine to give themselves a sense of stability through creating reliable means of expressing themselves, getting exercise, and setting boundaries for themselves yet, they're also just going through the motions. Could complacency really be an answer to the existential never-ending road we also walk on? And lastly, James' approach of constant vigilance, problem solving, and plan setting did ultimately get him the furthest toward the "goal" of escape.

The story follows the plight of Tyler, a "blue-collar type...and unspoken leader of the group" ('It Ends' Review - Inventive Horror Hangout Movie Gets Existential, written by Meagan Navarro of Bloody Disgusting), played by Mitchell Cole; aimless Pals Day (Akira Jackson) and Fisher (Noah Toth); and their blunt and posturing future systems engineer James (Phinehas Yoon), as they traverse this seemingly endless road, trying to gather their bearings and find a way out of this dreary yet verdant Purgatory.

We watch our heroes not necessarily survive, but learn to adapt to their new world, each in their own specific way. Tyler's approach is to tough out the trip, never revealing his true anxieties and fears, eventually culminating in him being the first to depart from the group, setting the tone for the rest of the film as the troupe must figure out how to fend for themselves without their faithful leader. Day and Fisher's approach is to accept the pointlessness of their endeavor and establish concrete routines and boundaries to ensure their mental and physical well-being. Meanwhile, our reluctant hero James views the entire scenario as an elaborate puzzle or test, designed to teach an invisible answer that never quite reveals itself.

If any of these wonderfully deep and fleshed-out characters, with their natural banter and camaraderie, feel familiar, it's because they do. Not in the "woah, they like me for real" type of way, but in a deeply personal "wow, this is how I approach life" kind of way. The film goes to great lengths to show how each traveler's approach is both valid and flawed at the same time. Tyler's brute-force method was effective at the start of the adventure, and his silent show of strength gave a sense of stability to the rest of the group. However, this avoidance of talking about his problems eventually bubbled over until he could no longer endure the incessant traveling, choosing to end his journey on his own terms by exiting the vehicle, leaving James the most affected by this loss. Day and Fisher's approach provides a much-needed and healthy routine to create a sense of stability through reliable means of expression, exercise, and boundary-setting for their trip. However, I have problems with this approach as well as they are doing what's considered healthy and normal in modern society but they're also just going through the motions. Can complacency really be the best approach to the existential never-ending road we call life? Is living life without any real purpose actually meaningful? Great coping mechanism yes, but a solution? I'm not really sure.

Lastly, James' approach of constant vigilance, problem solving, and plan setting ultimately gets him the furthest toward the "goal" of escape they all sought. However, this also leads him to abandon Day and Fisher to continue the journey, only to reach a literal Dead End (see what I did there 😉?). This reveal definitely seemed to be divisive amongst viewers because, upon reaching the end of the road, James ends up driving back the opposite way to find the friends he left behind, picking up a new companion and starting the same conversation he had with his friends at the beginning of the film. So, what was the point of the movie, if it had a point at all?

Analysis:

Truthfully, I don't believe any of these approaches (and, for that matter, my personal take lol) are right nor are they wrong. They're just simply different, common approaches to life that we see everyone take. I absolutely loved that even at the end of the road we see that SO MANY CARS have also reached this point as well, with no passengers inside them, leaving us, the viewer, to believe they all succumbed to the odd fate expected from everyone on this road, becoming zombies who only awaken upon hearing of other people who may provide them a means of escape, only to be relegated back to dormancy once this means of escape disappears. Because, yeah, life is bleak, it is seemingly endless, and it often times never gives you the straight answer you're looking for.

Likes and dislikes:

I'll just get this out of the way, I had no dislikes for this film. I rarely (yeah, I know this is my second review, let me cook, dang it!) rate films 5 stars. The only other film that I'd rate 5 stars is Life is Beautiful, and it's BECAUSE IT'S LIFE IS BEAUTIFUL (go watch it! Written and also directed by the lead actor Roberto Benigni). So, here goes my glazing session for this film:

Cinematography: Same as above, no dislikes and all five stars.

Acting: Listen, have you heard of any of these names before? Let me play it back for ya: Mitchell Cole (Tyler), Akira Jackson (Pals Day), Noah Toth (Fisher), and Phinehas Yoon (James) REMEMBER THESE NAMES because I have never seen such a talented young cast. They all nailed their roles. I loved the aloof, blunt directness Phinehas gave his James. I loved the stoic, quiet strength, with subtle vulnerability Mitchell gave Tyler, and I absolutely ADORED the heart and warmth Akira and Noah gave their Day and Fisher. If the phrase is "to chew a scene," then these peeps FEASTED.

Dialogue: Listen, have you heard of any of these names before? Let me play it back for ya: Mitchell Cole (Tyler), Akira Jackson (Pals Day), Noah Toth (Fisher), and Phinehas Yoon (James) REMEMBER THESE NAMES because I have never seen such a talented young cast. They all nailed their roles. They delivered each line with precision, emotion, and presence.

Bonus: I'd be remiss if I didn't mention how much I LOVE that this film does not shy away from its obvious inspiration: Dead End. I'm not going to say more than that since this review is already pretty lengthy, but you should also definitely give that film a watch too!

reviews.text: Do NOT Waste Your Time Honestly? Why did they even bother filming this? This was easily one of the worst movies I have ever watched. What was the point? No plot. No real storyline to speak of. No climax. No outcome. No reason. No explanation. Nothing. This was 90 mins of my life I will never get back. The movie just ends with no conclusion. It was so dumb. It could have been a great movie if they would have cut the boring dialog and useless banter. Do more with the people rushing the Jeep. Make a story out of a haunted forest or something. Tell us what happens to the characters. If you like a solid conclusion to wrap up a story then don't bother with this film. BTW any reviews saying this is a 10? They gotta be fake. On the up side: Akira Jackson had some great acting moments. I can see her moving on to better projects. She was the best of the line up. Mitchell Cole did a great job and I hope to see him on the screen again. I can see him moving on to bigger films as long as this one doesn't keep him back. Phinehas Yoon and Noah Toth were also decent actors. And please do not watch this thinking it is a horror. I have no idea why they called it that. It is barely a thriller. In fact I think the correct category for this film is to call it a BORE-ER.

reviews.text: Wow. All buildup; no payoff. Wow. What a complete waste of time. The setup is good, and it gets off to an exciting start, but unlike the Jeep, it rapidly runs out of gas. There's only one really likable character, played by Mitchell Cole, but by the middle of the film, he's no longer part of the ensemble. After that, it's just a matter of waiting for the figurative (and literal) end of the road. There are no answers to the central premise; for all I know, the writer didn't know how to give it a satisfactory ending. Just don't bother with this one.

reviews.author: alisonc-1
reviews.text: Absolutely Excellent Four friends have helped someone move, and Tyler (Mitchell Cole) offers to drive the other three - Day (Akira Jackson), Fisher (Noah Toth) and James (Phinehas Yoon) - to wherever they need to go, but somehow they miss a turn and find themselves stuck on a road that never seems to end. They can tell that time passes, as the sun rises and sets, night falls and morning comes, but they don't seem to feel sleepy, or hungry, or much of anything really. All they can do is to keep driving, as they try to figure out what is going on.... This sounds like a simple premise, and perhaps an obvious one: the friends are Gen Z, they've just finished college and are starting out for the "real" world (although Tyler is already there), and of course, what's the endless road ahead of them but the future? But this movie is so much more than that - the dialogue is both funny, poignant and very realistic, the relationships between these young people are completely believable, the hypotheses that they consider and discard and consider again are all things you would hope for in this type of scenario. The actors are all terrific here, and the very enclosed set (a road, a vehicle, some trees) is used to great effect. In the end, the story speaks to every generation, and it is up to each viewer to decide how to parse the film, but I found it utterly wonderful. Probably my favorite film of the year; highly recommended!
